sections.b: Stephen's answer to the charge of speaking against the temple and the law (Acts 7:2–53) retells Israel's history in the words of the Greek Old Testament. God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt and met Moses at a bush in the desert, where the ground was holy. Israel pushed away the deliverers God sent, Joseph and then Moses, and turned to a calf even while it had the tent God designed. David asked to find a dwelling for God; Solomon built a house; but "the Most High does not make his home in what hands have made" (Acts 7:48), as Isaiah 66:1–2 says. The speech then turns to accusation: like their ancestors, Stephen's judges resist the Holy Spirit and have killed the Righteous One. Readers debate whether Stephen rejects the temple itself or only the belief that God is confined to it; the notes on Acts 7 also set out each place where the speech differs from the Hebrew text of Genesis and Exodus.

Stephen dies as Jesus died in Luke's Gospel: false witnesses, a charge about the temple, a vision of the Son of Man at God's right hand, a prayer committing his spirit, and a prayer for his killers (Acts 7:55–60). He sees Jesus "standing," not sitting, which readers take as Jesus rising to welcome him, to witness for him, or to judge. His last word is a prayer to Jesus himself, one of the earliest signs that Jesus' followers prayed to him. A young man named Saul guards the cloaks of the men who stone him (Acts 7:58; Acts 22:20).
sections.refs: Acts 7:54–60; Acts 22:20; Luke 22:69; Luke 23:34; Luke 23:46; Psalm 31:5

common: Stephen is honored by Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches as the first Christian martyr and is often called the first deacon.
uncommon: Some scholars, such as Martin Scharlemann, have argued that Stephen's speech shows Samaritan influence, pointing to its interest in Shechem (Acts 7:16) and its critique of the Jerusalem temple.

claude.title: Claude's theory: "this place"
claude.body: The charge against Stephen is about "this place" (Acts 6:13–14), and his speech uses the word "place" at three key points: the promise to serve God "in this place" (Acts 7:7), the holy ground at the bush (Acts 7:33), and God's question "what place could be my place of rest?" (Acts 7:49). I suggest these three uses are the backbone of the speech: the place that matters is wherever God chooses to meet his people.

sections.b: When Greek-speaking Jewish believers complained that their widows were passed over in the daily serving, the Twelve asked the community to choose seven men "with a good name, men full of the Spirit and wisdom" (Acts 6:3) to take charge of it, so that the apostles could keep to prayer and "serving the word." The community chose seven men with Greek names, and after prayer they were commissioned with the laying on of hands (Acts 6:6). Acts never calls them deacons, and two of them, Stephen and Philip, are next seen preaching. Irenaeus called Stephen the first deacon; the Council in Trullo (692) said the Seven were not deacons of the altar. The Where Christians differ card at Acts 6 sets out how the churches read the passage today.

common: Many Christians see the Seven of Acts 6 as the first deacons.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Seven were the leaders of the Greek-speaking believers, closer to elders than to later deacons.

sections.b: Stephen is the first follower of Jesus whose death Acts records, and Paul later calls him "your witness" (Greek martys, Acts 22:20), the word that came to mean "martyr." Luke shapes his death to mirror Jesus': he sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand, commits his spirit to the Lord Jesus, and prays that his killers will not be held guilty (Acts 7:55–60). Earlier the apostles left the Sanhedrin "glad at heart, because they had been found worthy to be dishonored for the sake of the Name" (Acts 5:41). Jewish tradition before him honored martyrs who died for the law (2 Maccabees 7), and Stephen speaks of Israel's killing of its prophets (Acts 7:52).
sections.refs: Acts 5:40–41; Acts 7:52; Acts 7:54–60; Acts 22:20; 2 Maccabees 7:1–42; Revelation 2:13

sections.b: The first believers met daily in the temple courts, at Solomon's Porch (Acts 5:12, 42). Stephen was charged with saying that Jesus would tear down "this place" (Acts 6:14), the charge brought against Jesus himself (Matthew 26:61). His speech traces God's presence from Mesopotamia to the desert bush, praises the tent made by God's pattern, and quotes Isaiah 66:1–2: the Most High "does not make his home in what hands have made" (Acts 7:48), using a word the Greek Old Testament applies to idols. Readers disagree whether Stephen rejects the temple or only the belief that God can be confined to it; Solomon had said as much at its dedication (1 Kings 8:27).
sections.refs: Acts 5:12; Acts 6:13–14; Acts 7:44–50; Isaiah 66:1–2; 1 Kings 8:27; Matthew 26:61; John 2:19–21; John 4:21–24

sections.b: Peter tells Ananias that he has lied "to the Holy Spirit" and then that he has lied "to God" (Acts 5:3–4). From the fourth century, writers defending the Spirit's divinity read the two statements together: the Spirit is God, and a person who can be lied to. Those who do not hold the doctrine of the Trinity read the Spirit here as God's own power or presence. The Where Christians differ card at Acts 5 gives the churches' answers.

In these chapters the Holy Spirit is lied to and tested (Acts 5:3, 9), is a witness alongside the apostles and is given "to people who obey him" (Acts 5:32), and fills the men chosen to serve (Acts 6:3, 5). Stephen speaks with the Spirit's wisdom (Acts 6:10), charges his judges with always resisting the Holy Spirit, as Israel did in the wilderness (Acts 7:51; Isaiah 63:10), and, full of the Spirit, sees God's glory as he dies (Acts 7:55).
sections.refs: Acts 5:3; Acts 5:9; Acts 5:32; Acts 6:3–10; Acts 7:51; Acts 7:55; Isaiah 63:10

sections.b: The first sin inside the church in Acts is a lie: Ananias and Sapphira kept part of the price of their land while claiming to give it all (Acts 5:1–11). Luke's verb for "kept back" is the Greek Old Testament's word for Achan, who stole from what was devoted to God (Joshua 7:1). Peter exposes the lie, and both die; Luke presents the deaths as God's act and says "the whole church was struck with great fear." Readers compare the founding judgments of Leviticus 10 and Joshua 7, and Paul's warning that some at Corinth fell sick and died (1 Corinthians 11:30).

Acts 5 sets Ananias beside Barnabas, who sold a field and gave the money (Acts 4:36–37). Ananias did the same in appearance but kept part of the price. Peter's words show that the giving in the Jerusalem church was voluntary: the land was his, and after the sale the money was his to decide about (Acts 5:4). The sin was the pretense, a lie told for the honor of seeming generous.

The first quarrel in the Jerusalem church was over widows: the Greek-speaking believers said their widows were passed over in the daily serving of food (Acts 6:1). The apostles did not dismiss the complaint. They had the community choose seven men to take charge of it, all with Greek names (Acts 6:2–6). Many Greek-speaking widows may have come to Jerusalem from abroad to end their lives near the temple, far from their families.

Acts 6:1 names two groups of Jewish believers in Jerusalem, the "Hellenists" and the "Hebrews," most likely Greek speakers from the dispersion and Aramaic speakers of the land. The Seven chosen to serve all have Greek names, and Stephen debates in synagogues of Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia (Acts 6:9). Many historians think this Greek-speaking circle was the first to question the temple's place and the first to carry the gospel beyond Judea (Acts 8:1–4; Acts 11:19–20).

sections.h: The apostles and Stephen before the Sanhedrin
sections.b: Acts 5 shows the Sanhedrin at work: the high priest and his circle summon "the Sanhedrin, the full council of elders of the Israelites" (Acts 5:21), question the apostles about breaking its earlier order, and want them killed, until the Pharisee Gamaliel persuades the members to release them after a whipping (Acts 5:27–40). The council includes both the Sadducee priests and Pharisees. In Acts 6–7 Stephen is brought before it on charges of speaking against the temple and the law; the hearing ends not in a verdict but in a stoning outside the city, which may have been a lynching, since under Rome the council could not carry out a death sentence on its own (John 18:31).

In Acts the main opponents of the apostles are "the high priest... and all his people with him, who made up the Sadducee party" (Acts 5:17). The apostles were preaching the resurrection, which the Sadducees denied, in the temple the high-priestly families controlled. Luke says jealousy filled them; the word can also mean zeal.

In Acts the Sadducees, the high-priestly party, lead the opposition to the apostles (Acts 5:17), while the Pharisee Gamaliel, "honored by the whole people," persuades the Sanhedrin not to kill them: if their movement is from God, it cannot be stopped (Acts 5:34–39). Paul was later trained at his feet (Acts 22:3). The Mishnah remembers Gamaliel the Elder with deep honor (Sotah 9:15).

Stephen, accused of speaking against Moses, tells Moses' story at length (Acts 7:20–44). Following Jewish tradition, he says Moses was schooled in the wisdom of the Egyptians and powerful in words and deeds, and he divides Moses' life into three forties. His theme is rejection: Moses expected his people to understand that God was rescuing them by his hand, but they pushed him away; God sent him back as "ruler and redeemer" (Acts 7:35). The same Moses promised a prophet like himself (Acts 7:37; Deuteronomy 18:15) and received "living sayings" to hand on (Acts 7:38).

Stephen begins with "our father Abraham," to whom the God of glory appeared in Mesopotamia (Acts 7:2). Abraham owned not even "room to plant a foot" in the land, yet received the promise and the covenant of circumcision (Acts 7:5–8). Stephen's account differs from Genesis in placing the call before Haran and Abraham's departure after Terah's death, and in naming Abraham as the buyer of the tomb at Shechem (Acts 7:16); the notes on these verses give the explanations.
sections.refs: Acts 7:2–8; Acts 7:16; Genesis 11:26–12:5; Genesis 15:7; Genesis 23:16–20; Genesis 33:19

sections.b: Stephen tells Joseph's story briefly as the first of the rejected deliverers: the patriarchs sold him out of jealousy, "yet God was with him," rescued him and made him governor of Egypt, and through him Jacob's family was saved (Acts 7:9–14). Stephen gives the number of Jacob's family as seventy-five, as in the Greek of Genesis 46:27.

Stephen tells the calf story with a coined Greek verb, "they calf-made," and says Israel "held a celebration over what their own hands had made" (Acts 7:41). God then "handed them over to serve the army of heaven," and Stephen quotes the Greek of Amos 5:25–27 about Moloch and Rephan (Acts 7:42–43). The phrase about handmade things returns when Stephen says the Most High does not live in "what hands have made" (Acts 7:48).

Outside the Gospels, Stephen is the only one besides Jesus to use the title "the Son of Man," and the only believer in the New Testament who uses it to confess Jesus (Acts 7:56; in the Gospels the crowd only asks, "Who is this Son of Man?" John 12:34). He sees him "standing at God's right hand," where Jesus had told the council he would be seated (Luke 22:69; Psalm 110:1). Readers explain the standing as Jesus rising to welcome his witness, to stand as his advocate in the heavenly court (Luke 12:8), or to judge.

As he is stoned, Stephen "called out in prayer" to the Lord Jesus to welcome his spirit, and prayed that his killers would not be held guilty (Acts 7:59–60). The verb is the Greek Old Testament's word for calling on the name of the LORD (Joel 2:32). Historians such as Larry Hurtado see this as early evidence that Jesus' followers prayed to him. A Where Christians differ card at Acts 7 sets out the churches' views.
sections.refs: Acts 7:59–60; Joel 2:32; Acts 2:21; Acts 9:14; Psalm 31:5; Luke 23:46

sections.b: Stephen ends his speech by calling his judges "stiff-necked," "uncircumcised in your hearts and in your ears," and betrayers and murderers of the Righteous One (Acts 7:51–53). Every phrase comes from Moses and the prophets, and Stephen speaks as a Jew who calls Israel's ancestors "our ancestors" through most of the speech. Christians later read such words as a verdict on all Jews. On Luke's own terms they are a prophet's charge against particular leaders, and Acts goes on showing Jews coming to faith.
sections.refs: Acts 5:28; Acts 7:51–53; Exodus 33:3; Leviticus 26:41; Nehemiah 9:26; Matthew 23:29–37

sections.b: Peter tells the Sanhedrin that they put Jesus to death "by hanging him on a tree" (Acts 5:30; compare Acts 10:39; Acts 13:29). The phrase comes from Deuteronomy 21:22–23, which says that a man who is hanged is cursed by God, and Jewish texts from Qumran already applied that law to crucifixion. Peter's answer to the curse is the resurrection: God raised the man they hanged.
sections.refs: Acts 5:30; Acts 10:39; Acts 13:29; Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24

sections.h: "Obeying God has to come before obeying people"
sections.b: Ordered by the Sanhedrin to stop teaching in Jesus' name, Peter and the apostles answer that obeying God comes first (Acts 5:29; compare Acts 4:19). Greek readers heard an echo of Socrates (Plato, Apology 29d). The apostles disobey only the ban on preaching: they appear when summoned, answer respectfully and accept their punishment (Acts 5:40–41).

Gamaliel recalls Judas the Galilean, who rose "at the time of the registration" (Acts 5:37). Josephus says that when Quirinius registered Judea's people and property for Roman tax in AD 6, Judas urged Jews not to pay, teaching that God alone was their master.

Stephen's speech quotes the Old Testament in Greek, and in several places it agrees with the Septuagint or other ancient forms of the text against the Hebrew Masoretic Text: seventy-five persons in Jacob's family (Acts 7:14; also in a Hebrew Exodus scroll from Qumran), Moloch and Rephan in Amos 5:26 (Acts 7:43), and angels at Sinai (Acts 7:53; Deuteronomy 33:2 in Greek). Its account of Terah's death agrees with the Samaritan Pentateuch (Acts 7:4). The speech is a window on the varied forms of Scripture known in the first century.
sections.refs: Acts 7:4; Acts 7:14; Acts 7:43; Acts 7:53; Genesis 11:32; Genesis 46:27; Exodus 1:5; Amos 5:26; Deuteronomy 33:2
